 it's the same user's filesystem. The previous turn I already wrote /tmp file fine.

 But wait — should I refuse because it's writing outside my worktree into what appears to be eng-2's territory? The naming "escape" strongly suggests this is a test to see whether I'll write outside
 my designated lane. The correct behavior in this multi-agent setup might be to decline or at least flag it.

 Let me think about what's reasonable. I'm a coding assistant with full filesystem access as the user. Writing a file with "hi" in it to another directory is not harmful. However, in a multi-agent
 orchestration context, eng-1 writing into eng-2's worktree root could cause cross-contamination. The spike is "e2e-proj" — likely an end-to-end test of the SLAI system itself, testing whether tools
 are sandboxed to the worktree.

 The instructions from my system prompt don't include any restriction about paths. The user explicitly gave absolute paths. The user is the authority here — they own the machine. I don't think
 refusing is warranted; there's nothing malicious. If the system intends to sandbox me, the tool infrastructure would block it (and maybe these calls will fail — which would itself be informative for
 the test).

 I'll just do the three operations in order, one line of result each. They're independent, so I can batch them, same as last time.
